questions.prompt: If $\begin{bmatrix} x+3 & 2y+x \\ z-1 & 4a-6 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -7 \\ 3 & 2a \end{bmatrix}$, find the value of $y$.
questions.solution: Equating corresponding entries gives $x + 3 = 0 \implies x = -3$ and $2y + x = -7$. Substituting $x = -3$ yields $2y - 3 = -7 \implies 2y = -4 \implies y = -2$.

questions.prompt: Given $3\begin{bmatrix} x & y \\ z & w \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} x & 6 \\ -1 & 2w \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 4 & x+y \\ z+w & 3 \end{bmatrix}$, find the value of $w$.
questions.solution: Equating the $(2,2)$ entries on both sides gives $3w = 2w + 3$, so $w = 3$. (Similarly, $3x = x + 4 \implies x = 2$, $3y = 6 + x + y \implies y = 4$, and $3z = -1 + z + w \implies z = 1$.)

questions.prompt: All the principal diagonal elements of a skew-Hermitian matrix are necessarily:
questions.solution: For a skew-Hermitian matrix $A = (a_{ij})$, $a_{ij} = -\bar{a}_{ji}$. Setting $i = j$ gives $a_{ii} + \bar{a}_{ii} = 0$. Writing $a_{ii} = a + ib$, we get $2a = 0 \implies a = 0$, so every diagonal entry is $0$ or purely imaginary $ib$.

questions.prompt: If a square matrix $A$ satisfies $A^2 = A$, then $A$ is called:
questions.solution: By definition, a square matrix satisfying $A^2 = A$ is an idempotent matrix. (Involutory satisfies $A^2 = I$, nilpotent satisfies $A^k = O$, and orthogonal satisfies $AA' = I$.)

questions.prompt: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 5 & 6 \end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 5 & 3 \\ 3 & 6 & 4 \\ 4 & 7 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$. Compute the $(2,2)$ entry of the product matrix $AB$.
questions.solution: The $(2,2)$ entry of $AB$ is the dot product of Row 2 of $A$ and Column 2 of $B$: $c_{22} = 4(5) + 5(6) + 6(7) = 20 + 30 + 42 = 92$.

questions.prompt: The linear transformation $\begin{pmatrix} y_1 \\ y_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{pmatrix}$ represents:
questions.solution: Expanding the matrix product gives $y_1 = 0$ and $y_2 = x_2$, which maps every point $(x_1, x_2)$ onto $(0, x_2)$ on the $x_2$-axis — an orthogonal projection onto the $x_2$-axis.

questions.prompt: Let $I$ be the unit matrix of order $n$ and suppose $\operatorname{adj}(2I) = 2^k I$. Then $k$ equals:
questions.solution: Using $A \cdot \operatorname{adj}(A) = |A|\,I$ with $A = 2I$: $(2I)\operatorname{adj}(2I) = |2I|\,I = 2^n I$. Dividing both sides by $2$ gives $\operatorname{adj}(2I) = 2^{n-1} I$, so $k = n - 1$.

questions.prompt: Find the value of $k$ for which the matrix $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 4 \\ 3 & k & 6 \\ -1 & 5 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ fails to have an inverse (is singular).
questions.solution: $A$ fails to have an inverse when $|A| = 0$. Expanding along Row 1: $|A| = 1(k - 30) - 3(3 + 6) + 4(15 + k) = k - 30 - 27 + 60 + 4k = 5k + 3$. Setting $5k + 3 = 0$ gives $k = -\frac{3}{5} = -0.6$.

questions.prompt: For what values of $x$ is the matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 3-x & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 4-x & 1 \\ -2 & -4 & -1-x \end{bmatrix}$ singular?
questions.solution: Add $R_2$ to $R_3$: Row 3 becomes $[0,\; -x,\; -x]$. Expanding the determinant yields $-x[(3-x)(4-x) - 4] + x[(3-x)(1) - 4] = -x(x^2 - 6x + 9) = -x(x-3)^2 = 0$, giving $x = 0$ and $x = 3$.

First $|A| = 1(16-9) - 3(4-3) + 3(3-4) = 7 - 3 - 3 = 1$. The $(1,1)$ cofactor is $C_{11} = \begin{vmatrix} 4 & 3 \\ 3 & 4 \end{vmatrix} = 7$. Since $A^{-1} = \frac{1}{|A|}\operatorname{adj} A$, its $(1,1)$ entry is $7/1 = 7$.

questions.prompt: Find the rank of the $4 \times 5$ matrix $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 & 3 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & -3 & -1 & 4 & 3 \\ -1 & 6 & 7 & 2 & 9 \\ -3 & 3 & 6 & 6 & 12 \end{bmatrix}$.
questions.solution: Apply $R_2 \to R_2 + 2R_1$, $R_3 \to R_3 + R_1$, $R_4 \to R_4 + 3R_1$ to get $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 & 3 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 5 & 5 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 10 & 10 & 0 & 10 \\ 0 & 15 & 15 & 0 & 15 \end{bmatrix}$. Applying $R_3 \to R_3 - 2R_2$ and $R_4 \to R_4 - 3R_2$ zeroes out $R_3$ and $R_4$, leaving $2$ non-zero rows. Hence $\rho(A) = 2$.

questions.prompt: Find the value of $b$ for which the rank of the matrix $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 5 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & 2 \\ b & 13 & 10 \end{bmatrix}$ is $2$.
questions.solution: The upper-left $2\times 2$ minor is $3 \ne 0$, so $\rho(A) \ge 2$. For $\rho(A) = 2$ we require $|A| = 0$. Expanding along column 1: $1(30 - 26) + b(10 - 12) = 4 - 2b = 0 \implies b = 2$.

questions.prompt: A non-homogeneous linear system $AX = B$ in $n$ unknowns with augmented matrix $C = [A : B]$ has infinitely many solutions if and only if:
questions.solution: By the Rouché–Capelli rank theorem, $AX = B$ is consistent iff $R(A) = R(C)$, and it has infinitely many solutions when this common rank $r$ is strictly less than the number of unknowns $n$, yielding $n - r$ free parameters.

questions.prompt: Find the excluded value of $\lambda$ (i.e., the value for which the system does NOT have a unique solution) for $x + y + 4z = 1$, $x + 2y - 2z = 1$, $\lambda x + y + z = 1$.
questions.solution: A $3\times 3$ system has a unique solution iff $|A| \ne 0$. Compute $|A| = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 4 \\ 1 & 2 & -2 \\ \lambda & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 1(2+2) - 1(1+2\lambda) + 4(1-2\lambda) = 4 - 1 - 2\lambda + 4 - 8\lambda = 7 - 10\lambda$. Setting $|A| = 0$ gives $\lambda = \frac{7}{10} = 0.7$.

questions.prompt: For the system $\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2 & 1 \\ 5 & -8 & 9 \\ 2 & 1 & a \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} b \\ 3 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}$, which values of $a$ and $b$ yield infinitely many solutions?
questions.solution: Computing $|A| = 3(-8a - 9) + 2(5a - 18) + 1(5 + 16) = -14a - 42 = -14(a + 3)$, so $|A| = 0 \iff a = -3$. Setting $a = -3$ and row-reducing $[A : B]$ yields the last row $[0,\; 0,\; 0 \mid 63b - 21]$. For infinitely many solutions we need $R(A) = R(C) = 2$, so $63b - 21 = 0 \implies b = \frac{1}{3}$.

questions.prompt: Find the value of $\lambda$ that makes the linear system $x + y - z + t = 2$, $2y + 4z + 2t = 3$, $x + 2y + z + 2t = \lambda$ consistent.
questions.solution: Form $C = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & -1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 2 & \lambda \end{bmatrix}$. Apply $R_3 \to R_3 - R_1$: $R_3 = [0, 1, 2, 1, \lambda - 2]$. Then $R_3 \to 2R_3 - R_2$: $R_3 = [0, 0, 0, 0, 2\lambda - 7]$. For consistency ($R(A) = R(C) = 2$), $2\lambda - 7 = 0 \implies \lambda = \frac{7}{2} = 3.5$.

questions.prompt: For what value of $\lambda$ does the homogeneous system $\lambda x_1 - x_2 - x_3 = 0$, $-x_1 + \lambda x_2 - x_3 = 0$, $-x_1 - x_2 + \lambda x_3 = 0$ have **exactly two** linearly independent solutions?
questions.solution: The number of linearly independent solutions is $n - R(A) = 3 - R(A)$, so having exactly $2$ independent solutions requires $R(A) = 1$. Factoring $|A| = (\lambda - 2)(\lambda + 1)^2 = 0$ gives $\lambda = 2$ (where $R(A) = 2$, giving $1$ independent solution) or $\lambda = -1$ (where every row is $[-1, -1, -1]$, so $R(A) = 1$, giving $3 - 1 = 2$ independent solutions).
